title: Shorter Days Can Be Tough. Get Better Sleep With These White Noise Machines
gist: WIRED's buying guide to white noise machines ranks Hatch devices (Restore 3 at $170, Sleep Clock at $250) at the top while noting that much of Hatch's sound content sits behind a Hatch+ subscription. Budget and analog picks from Snooz, Momcozy, Restnature and HoMedics fill out the list.

insights.claim: The Hatch Restore 3, priced at $170, offers 58 sounds and multi-step sleep routines, but users need a subscription to access all of its content and options.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Consumer sleep hardware is being monetized through recurring subscriptions layered over the device sale.
insights.quote: Needs a subscription to access all content and options
insights.locator: Best White Noise Machine With Sunrise Clock

insights.claim: The $250 Hatch Sleep Clock combines a sunrise alarm, bedside light, sound machine and contactless motion-based sleep tracking, and its sleep data is accessible without a Hatch+ subscription, though its audio library requires one.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Hatch is bundling categories (alarm, light, tracker) into one premium-priced device to move up the price ladder.
insights.quote: Sleep data is accessible without a Hatch+ subscription
insights.locator: Best White Noise Machine With Sleep Tracking

insights.claim: A Hatch+ subscription unlocks more than 2,500 sounds, stories and meditations on the Sleep Clock, positioning content as the paid upsell on top of the hardware.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: The size of the content library is the lever for subscription conversion in sleep devices.

insights.claim: The Hatch Sleep Clock tracks sleep without cameras or microphones and offers no physiological data, snoring detection or audio-based insights, unlike wearable trackers.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Privacy-first passive tracking is a selling point but caps data richness versus wearables.
insights.quote: No camera or microphone is recording your nights

insights.claim: Hatch is phasing out its older Hatch Rest and replacing it with the $80 Hatch Baby Sound Machine, which comes bundled with a promotional Hatch+ subscription.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Subscription trials bundled at purchase are Hatch's funnel for recurring revenue, starting with parents.
insights.quote: As Hatch phases out the older Hatch Rest
insights.locator: Best White Noise Machine for Kids

insights.claim: The Snooz machine, at $100, generates its noise with a real fan and offers only one sound, which WIRED flags as a higher price for a single feature.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: A simple single-function device can still command premium pricing through design differentiation.
insights.quote: Higher price tag, one singular feature

insights.claim: Portable budget machines from Momcozy ($28) and Restnature (discounted to $17) cover the low end of the category with night-lights, Bluetooth or USB-C charging.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: The low end of the category is commoditized and heavily discounted, pressuring premium brands to justify price.
insights.locator: Best White Noise Machine for Infants

insights.claim: The author's $25 HoMedics SoundSleep machine has worked for over a decade, though its battery operation and volume have degraded over time.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Durable cheap hardware limits replacement cycles in the category.
insights.quote: Has worked well for over a decade

insights.claim: WIRED notes that a desk or box fan can stand in for a white noise machine in a pinch, with a dedicated sound machine preferred only for those wanting a wider range of sounds or not wanting to cool the room.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Free substitutes cap the addressable market for basic sound machines.
insights.locator: Does a Fan Make a Good White Noise Machine?

insights.claim: When buying a sound machine for a child or baby, WIRED advises keeping volume to no more than 50 decibels and placing the machine more than 200 centimeters (6.5 feet) from where the child sleeps.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Child-safety guidelines shape product design and marketing for the infant segment.
insights.quote: keep sound machines to no more than 50 decibels

insights.claim: Pink and brown noise sit at the lower end of the sound spectrum, are less grating than pure white noise, and have been found to help people sleep a little more deeply, which is why machines often bundle several noise colors.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Feature bundling of multiple noise colors is now table stakes in the category.

insights.claim: WIRED says it receives a small cut of most sales when readers click through to buy recommended products, while stating that revenue does not influence its choices.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Commerce-affiliate revenue is a core monetization channel for digital publishers.
insights.locator: How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?
